The daily work of farmworkers, farm, ranch, and aquacultural animals centers on the daily cycle of animal care: feed and water animals according to formulas and schedules and check feed and water supplies; herd, rotate grazing, or move animals according to plan, driving them to weighing, loading, or pens; observe feed intake, rumination, body condition, and behavior, identify disease, injury, or abnormal signs, and handle them per instructions or call a veterinarian; assist with births and complete identification and grouping according to rules; perform production tasks such as milking, egg collection, and shearing; administer medications, vaccines, or pesticides according to labels and veterinary requirements and carry out cleaning and disinfection; clean barns, pens, and equipment and check and repair fences, housing, and machinery; record growth, feeding, production, and cost information.

paragraphs:
Work context｜Farmworkers, farm, ranch, and aquacultural animals work at sites such as barns, pens, grazing land, and milking parlors, forming a daily care cycle around feeding and watering, grazing and moving herds, health observation and handling, reproduction and identification, production tasks, and cleaning and facilities.
Work location｜Dairy farms, beef cattle and sheep grazing land, pig farms and poultry houses, stables, aquaculture ponds and hatcheries, and feed rooms and storage areas.

Work conditions｜Mainly physical work combining outdoor and indoor settings (in the O*NET work context, 65% report daily "outdoors, exposed to all weather conditions" work), requiring prolonged standing (continually or almost continually 49%) and walking (continually or almost continually 41%); work schedules are mainly regular (53%), with seasonal and irregular each about 23%, and 42% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week; there may be exposure to dust, odors, disinfectants, and animal waste.

Main objects｜Live animals such as cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry, equines, fish and shellfish, and bee colonies, feed and additives, water and housing facilities, animal medications and vaccines, and records and production data.
Collaboration｜Collaborate with farm managers, veterinarians and breeding technicians, feed and equipment suppliers, and staff in transport and slaughter and processing.

Tools and materials｜Feeding and watering equipment, milking and egg collection equipment, pen and fence tools, cleaning and disinfection equipment, machinery such as tractors and feed wagons, and production and feeding record sheets.
Institutional basis｜Label and veterinary rules for animal medications and vaccines, animal welfare and transport requirements, barn and environmental safety requirements, employment and wage and hour rules, and local requirements on agricultural employment and employment status (the United States has separate H-2A employment and employer responsibility requirements for temporary or seasonal agricultural workers).
Record requirements｜Feeding and production records, animal health and medication records, and reproduction and herd movement records must be documented as required.

Safety and jurisdictional boundaries｜Animal medication and handling, zoonotic disease protection, machinery and pen safety, and employment status must follow labels, veterinary and employer rules, and local laws; questions involving medication, animal disease, and employment status must be confirmed by a veterinarian or the competent authority, and this page does not provide veterinary, medication, or legal advice.

entries.answer: Care for live animals on farms, ranches, grazing areas and aquaculture operations, including cattle, sheep, pigs, goats, equines, poultry, rabbits, fish, shellfish and bees: feed and water according to formulas, drive and rotate grazing, milk, weigh, catch and load; observe animals to detect disease and injury, administer medication, vaccines or pesticides according to labels and veterinary requirements and assist with calving; group and identify animals by weight, age and body condition; clean and maintain barns, pens and equipment and inspect and repair fences and implements; and record growth, feeding, yield and cost information.
entries.question: What do farmworkers, farm, ranch, and aquacultural animals mainly do?

entries.answer: The objects of responsibility differ: this occupation mainly cares directly for live animals and completes feeding, grazing, milking and health observation; crop, nursery and greenhouse farmworkers focus on crop production; agricultural equipment operators mainly operate tractors and large farm machinery; first-line supervisors of farming, fishing and forestry workers assign tasks and supervise work quality and safety; animal disease diagnosis and treatment is borne by veterinarians; farm labor contractors organize and settle the employment of others; and farmers and agricultural managers are responsible for business decisions and finances.

BLS notes that the typical entry-level education for this occupation requires no formal educational credential and no related work experience, with short-term on-the-job training provided. Work involving animal medication, vaccines and milking equipment operation also requires specialized training according to labels, veterinary advice and equipment procedures; animal disease diagnosis and treatment must be borne by a veterinarian holding a practice qualification. entries.answer: A more accurate judgment is that some tasks will be assisted by tools and that the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation and structural adjustment. A 2023 ILO study shows that task exposure varies widely across occupations and that technical feasibility does not mean employers have already adopted it; meanwhile feeding and grazing work, animal health observation, medication and handling, and machinery and barn safety require on-site work and responsibility, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change rather than that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution of practitioners within the same statistical period, not a starting salary. This occupation commonly has fixed schedules plus seasonal and irregular arrangements, and some posts provide living on site and meals; personal income must be judged together with the pay method (hourly, piece rate or live-on-site lump sum) and actual hours worked (O*NET work context shows 42% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week).

entries.answer: Yes. BLS notes that the typical entry-level education for this occupation requires no formal educational credential and no related work experience, with short-term on-the-job training provided, and most posts are taken up through mentoring. However, posts involving animal medication, handling and equipment operation usually require specialized training; animal disease diagnosis and treatment must be borne by a licensed veterinarian. Whether it is feasible depends on the target employer and local provisions. United States agricultural employment is subject to federal rules such as MSPA regarding wages, housing, transport, disclosure and records, and temporary or seasonal agricultural employment also involves employer responsibilities and labor certification procedures under the H-2A program, and this page does not replace the original regulations.

details: The page explains that the H-2A program allows agricultural employers who anticipate a shortage of domestic labor to bring in nonimmigrant foreign workers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural labor or services.

subject.name: Farmworkers, Farm, Ranch, and Aquacultural Animals
subject.summary: Care for live animals on farms, ranches, grazing areas, and aquaculture operations, including cattle, sheep, pigs, goats, horses and other equines, poultry, rabbits, fish, shellfish, and bees, as well as animals raised for products such as meat, hides, wool, feathers, eggs, milk, and honey: feed and water animals according to formulas and schedules, herd and rotate grazing, milk, weigh, catch, and load animals; observe animals to detect disease and injury, administer medications, vaccines, or pesticides according to veterinary or label instructions, and assist with births; group animals by weight, age, and body condition, and tag, brand, or paint-mark them; clean and maintain barns, pens, and fences, and check and repair equipment, machinery, and facilities; record growth, feeding, production, and cost information.
